source: Wikipedia: Scenario planning (cites Kahn, Wack 1985, Schwartz 1991, Schoemaker 1993/1995, Diffenbach 1983, Shell 2008, Meinert 2014)
finding: Kahn at RAND in the 1950s wrote stories of the future as if told by people living in it. Berger built La Prospective in France. Wack began business scenarios at Shell in 1971, and the 1973 oil shock gave them force. Shell's six-step method is: drivers and assumptions, framework, 7 to 9 mini-scenarios, cut to 2 or 3, draft, identify issues.
numbers: Hudson Institute 1961; Wack at Shell 1971; shock 1973. Diffenbach 1983 survey: alternate scenarios were the third most used long-range technique, used by 68% of large organisations. Shell steps: 7 to 9 mini-scenarios cut to 2 or 3.
limits: Secondary source. It says the evidence of effect is only anecdotal and mostly from Shell. The page is tagged as needing citations.
agent_relevance: The agent's reframe operator can copy the funnel shape: widen to 7 to 9 candidate framings, then cut to 2 or 3 by a fixed rule, then draft each in full.

source: Wikipedia: Scenario planning, evidence and criticism section
finding: An early-1980s audit by de Geus's team found that decision making after the scenarios, not the scenarios, was the main cause of weak strategy implementation. Critics call the method subjective and untested. Scenarios can defeat themselves (a forecast changes the behaviour it predicts). Schwartz warns that giving scenarios probabilities makes people focus on the most likely one.
numbers: No effect sizes given. Only the 68% (1983) use figure and the 7 to 9 to 2 to 3 funnel.
limits: Anecdotal base; decades-long timescales make proof hard. Self-defeating-forecast point is from Overland 2019 as cited.
agent_relevance: Supports guardrail G5 (code selects) and the rule not to attach probabilities to reframings: keep scenario sets unranked, and test what the agent does after the reframe, not only the reframe itself.

source: Wack, P. (1985) Scenarios: Uncharted waters ahead. Harvard Business Review 63(5):72-89 (HBR landing page, intro only)
finding: Wack argues that forecasting worked in the stable 1950s and 1960s but that since the early 1970s forecast errors became more frequent and sometimes huge, so planning needs another tool. He was head of the business environment division of Shell's planning department and developed the Shell system with Edward Newland.
numbers: Date: Sept 1985 issue. He lectured on scenario planning at Harvard Business School in 1983 and 1984. No other numbers on the open page.
quote: forecasting errors have become more frequent
limits: Only the free opening paragraphs were readable. Concepts such as the microcosm, decision scenarios and the two kinds of scenario are not checked here.
agent_relevance: Motivates a scenario step when forecast error is high. Our agent should treat a single forecast as a risk, and use a scenario set only when a check shows its first framing is unstable.

source: Wilkinson, A. & Kupers, R. (2013) Living in the futures. Harvard Business Review, May 2013 (landing page, intro only)
finding: Before scenarios Shell used a computer system for cash-flow planning, the Unified Planning Machinery (UPM), introduced in 1965. Many commitments ran beyond its six-year horizon, it got even near-term forecasts wrong, and Shell shut it down in the early 1970s and began trying another approach.
numbers: UPM introduced 1965; horizon 6 years; closed early 1970s.
limits: Intro only. Authors are Shell insiders (Wilkinson was on the corporate scenario team for nearly a decade), so this is a participant account.
agent_relevance: Shows the origin as a failure of model-based point forecasting. For our agent: a precise model is not a substitute for generating alternative framings when the world shifts.

source: Wikipedia: Pierre Wack
finding: Wack (1922-1997) was a French oil executive and the first to use scenario planning in the private sector, at Shell's London headquarters in the 1970s. He wrote two 1985 HBR articles (Uncharted waters ahead; Shooting the rapids). The page says Shell anticipated two Arab-induced oil shocks in that decade. His later work for De Beers is flagged as needing a citation. Chermack (2017) wrote his biography.
numbers: Life 1922-1997; two HBR articles in 1985; 1970s Shell work.
limits: Wikipedia only. The claim that Shell anticipated both shocks has no measured outcome behind it.
agent_relevance: Background only. The 'anticipated the shock' story is the main evidence for the method and it is a single-firm anecdote, so the agent design should not lean on it.

source: Wikipedia: Herman Kahn
finding: Kahn at RAND applied game theory to nuclear war, and is named with Wack as a father of scenario planning. He published a 16-step escalation ladder in 1962 and a 44-step one by 1965, and books framed around scenarios (On Escalation, 1965; The Year 2000, 1967, with Wiener).
numbers: Hudson Institute founded 1961. On Thermonuclear War (1960) sold 14,000 copies in two months. Ladder 16 steps (1962) to 44 steps (1965).
limits: The page gives no formal definition of a scenario. The definition used in later work (Kahn and Wiener 1967) is quoted in a10.
agent_relevance: The escalation ladder is a staged state space with named rungs, close to our S0-S9 states. It shows the older form: scenarios as paths through enumerated steps, not free prose.

source: Wikipedia: Cross-impact analysis
finding: Cross-impact analysis was developed by Gordon and Helmer in 1966. Method: list 10 to 40 events, give each an initial probability, estimate a conditional probability for every pair, check the numbers for errors by repeated simulation, then run it to get scenarios. Intelligence-style versions use plus and minus signs instead of numbers.
numbers: First card game 'Future' at UCLA 1968; Institute for the Future added time series 1972; SMIC (Duperrin and Godet) 1974; Delphi plus cross-impact 1984. Gordon: 10 to 40 events.
limits: Futures-style version needs heavy maths and can produce impossible probabilities from negative impacts; intelligence-style results depend on the analysts and are hard to reproduce with a different group.
agent_relevance: The pairwise-conditional structure is a formal way to test whether a combination of assumptions is consistent. A program could do this check, which fits G5.

source: Wikipedia: Morphological analysis (problem-solving)
finding: Zwicky (Caltech astronomer) built the morphological box: list the dimensions of a problem, list options per dimension, then use cross-consistency assessment to delete combinations that cannot logically coexist. It is used for forecasting and policy analysis where causal models fail.
numbers: Worked example is a box with 6 categories and 4 options each. By simple arithmetic that is 4^6 = 4,096 combinations (not stated on the page).
limits: Page does not discuss scenario use or Ritchey's contribution in its body.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete way to turn 'drivers' into an enumerable space and prune it by a consistency table, which code can run without the model judging.

source: Wikipedia: Conjunction fallacy (Tversky and Kahneman 1983)
finding: Adding detail makes a story feel more probable while it is logically less probable. This is the behavioural reason Schoemaker and others warn that rich scenarios can raise confidence wrongly. Reformulating as counts out of 100 cuts the error.
numbers: Linda: 57% still erred when reworded 'whether or not'. Die sequence: 65% chose GRGRRR over RGRRR. Soviet invasion of Poland (1981 experts): joint event 4% vs 1% for the single event. Counts format (Gigerenzer 1991): errors fell from 85% to about 20%.
limits: Wikipedia gives no sample sizes. The Poland figure is a 1981 report, the counts figure is Gigerenzer 1991, not the 1983 paper.
agent_relevance: Direct caution for the draft step: a vivid, detailed scenario draft should never raise the agent's stated confidence. Rate plausibility by code over the skeleton, not by reading the prose.

source: Abdelwahed, Espasa & Meneguzzi (2026) Polyscene: Scenario planning as diversity planning. arXiv 2610.28102
finding: Casts scenario planning as a diversity planning problem. A scenario is a plan (narrative) from a stated present state; two scenarios differ if they end in different values on the analyst's drivers. Five criteria are coded as trajectory constraints (LTLf/PDDL3): plausible, internally consistent, relevant, challenging, and differentiated as a set. The engine, in Answer Set Programming (clingo), returns one scenario per reachable outcome within a cost budget, with no probabilities or ranking.
numbers: Geopolitics case: 6 countries, 65 action schemas over 20 CAMEO event types, board of 1 Jan 2021, budget 5 events: 8 outcomes, 5 of the 15 country pairs at war in the set; the abstract says each of the three wars that broke out by 1 Jan 2026 ends a scenario. Space is 2^15 war combinations versus the 4 themes of a workshop.
quote: a hypothetical sequence of events constructed to focus attention on causal processes and decision points
limits: New preprint (Oct 2026), code 'will be available upon publication'. Retrospective check only, on two hand-built domain models; the model of the topic is written by an analyst. Shows coverage, not that coverage helps a decision.
agent_relevance: This is the closest formal model to our reframe operator: enumerate structurally different endings by code under a budget, keep all, rank none. Matches G5 and avoids model-chosen 'most likely' futures.

source: Polyscene, Section 2 worked example: Shell's 1972 exercise as a planning problem
finding: Simplified Shell case: two drivers (does the cartel stay coordinated; does the region stay peaceful) give four outcomes. Shell's team examined two families: disruption (war, resupply of the ally, embargo that cuts the importer's capacity) and continuity (cartel coordination decays, peace, growth). The surprise-free projection, a united cartel in a peaceful region, was the conventional outcome the exercise was meant to challenge.
numbers: 2 drivers give 4 outcomes; 2 examined. With budget 3 the engine returns exactly two narratives, continuity and disruption.
limits: Authors say it is simplified and that the actors and events are theirs and follow the 1973 embargo; Shell's own scenarios were about producer revenues and supply, not war.
agent_relevance: Gives a small test case with a known answer for any reframe module: the right output must include the 'challenging' ending that differs from the conventional expectation.

source: Polyscene, Section 4 results and Table 5
finding: Outcome counts grow with budget; supply-chain boards give 3 outcomes in tiny time, the conflict board is heavy. Four shipping boards (Suez, Panama, Baltimore, Hormuz) at 1 Jan 2021: 3 outcomes each at budget 5. The Suez set holds the March 2021 blockage and the Red Sea diversion from Dec 2023 but misses the production stops of January 2024.
numbers: Conflicts board outcomes at budgets 4,5,6,7 read 5, 8, 9, 11 (table text garbled in extraction). Budget 5 run: 8.4 s; memory printed as '350 GB' (probably MB, unverified). Supply chain: 0.07 s, 36-37 MB. Means of 10 single-thread runs, Apple M1, clingo 5.8.2. Calibration: 8 pairs with clear relations; 1 misclassified (India-China).
limits: Many narratives differ only in event order, so search cost grows factorially with budget (authors' own limit). Single-thread runs return the same set; multi-thread may pick another narrative per outcome.
agent_relevance: Shows enumeration is cheap at small budget and explodes at larger ones, so our funnel (7 to 9 down to 2 or 3) must be budgeted by code, not left open.

source: Polyscene, Section 5 related work (taxonomy of automated scenario work)
finding: Four lines of automation: (1) consistency-based combination: cross-impact balance (Weimer-Jehle 2006) and computer-aided morphological analysis (Ritchey 2006); (2) speeding the manual exercise, e.g. NLP-built fuzzy cognitive maps (Davis 2022); (3) planning-based generation, the IBM Scenario Planning Advisor (Sohrabi et al. 2018), which costs actions by elicited likelihood then clusters plans; (4) LLM drafting (Ferrer i Pico 2025). Only planning-based systems return event sequences.
numbers: None numeric. Workshop output cited as three to five narratives (Amer et al. 2013).
limits: Authors' own framing; they argue LLM narratives read well but are neither guaranteed consistent nor grounded in a model of the topic.
agent_relevance: Our agent should use the model for drafting prose only after code has fixed the skeleton of each scenario, as in line (3) and the authors' argument against line (4).

source: Polyscene Section 1 on workshop bias and LLM narratives (secondary claims)
finding: States that scenario planning is meant to counter tunnel vision and anchoring, but the evidence that it does is mixed (citing Cordova-Pozo and Rouwette 2023), and that LLM-drafted narratives often fail to stay consistent (citing Simon, LLMs are incoherent storytellers) and can hallucinate.
numbers: No numbers given in this passage.
limits: These are citations passed on, not tested here. The two cited papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: A reason to run a code consistency check on any LLM scenario and to treat 'scenario planning reduces bias' as unproven for our agent (G1, G3).

source: Csaszar, Ketkar & Kim (2024) Artificial intelligence and strategic decision-making: evidence from entrepreneurs and investors. arXiv 2408.08811, section 2.1 scenario planning vignette
finding: GPT-4 was asked for one-sentence events that could make business schools obsolete and gave three scenarios (advanced personalised AI; employers prefer practical skills; students prefer micro-credentials). Asked for a plan for scenario 1 it gave six points, and named AI companies as a stakeholder without being asked. The authors say output is similar to what an MBA student could produce and that repeats appear after many scenarios.
numbers: 3 scenarios, 1 six-point plan. No scores. Single prompt.
limits: Illustration only, no evaluation, no human comparison.
agent_relevance: Shows LLMs can fill the 'generate several futures' slot cheaply. The open question is diversity and quality, which this vignette does not measure.

source: Csaszar et al. (2024), startup accelerator experiment (GPT-3.5 versus entrepreneurs)
finding: 250 evaluators with investment experience rated LLM-written and entrepreneur-written plans. LLM plans scored slightly higher. The gap was larger for plans the accelerator had rejected.
numbers: 309 plans received 2021-2022, 10 used (5 accepted, 5 rejected). Evaluators: US angel/VC/PE, mean 5 years investing. LLM plans +0.14 SD (p<0.001); item gaps 0.07 to 0.23 SD; +5 points recommend accepting (p=0.003); on rejected plans +7 points accept (p=0.003), +8 points intro (p=0.001), +6 points invest (p<0.001).
limits: Only 10 plans; GPT-3.5 chosen for context size; evaluators judge text, not outcomes. Not scenario planning itself.
agent_relevance: Evidence that LLM strategy text is rated at or above human text by experts, so ratings of fluency are a weak check. Needs ground-truth outcomes.

source: Csaszar et al. (2024), startup competition: LLM scores versus investor judges
finding: The LLM scored 138 business plans on the competition's own 10-item rubric and its scores correlated with investor judges at about the same level as judges with each other.
numbers: 731 plans over 10 cycles, 138 text-only (19%); 541 evaluations by 137 judges, 3 to 5 judges per plan; LLM scores averaged over 3 runs; average correlation LLM-judge 0.52, robust inside and after the training window.
limits: Agreement with judges is not accuracy against outcomes. Rubric of 10 items scored 0 to 100%.
agent_relevance: Shows an LLM can match human agreement on screening ideas. For scenario cutting, similar agreement is only a hint (G4), not proof.

source: Csaszar, Peterson & Wilde (2026) The strategic foresight of LLMs: evidence from a fully prospective venture tournament. arXiv 2602.01684
finding: Live Kickstarter projects launched after all model training cutoffs were ranked before outcomes were known. Frontier LLMs beat most human evaluators on rank correlation with realised funding.
numbers: 30 projects, 870 pairwise comparisons per LLM; humans: 346 experienced Prolific managers plus 3 MBA-trained investors. Spearman with outcome: Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.74; GPT-5 family 0.67-0.71; best human 0.45; other expert 0.04; Prolific crowd 0.19. Gemini minus best human 0.29 (p=0.063); minus crowd 0.55 (p=0.001).
limits: Draft marked do not cite; n = 30 projects; fundraising outcome is a narrow proxy for strategic foresight; bootstrap 90% intervals are wide. Evaluates judgment, not scenario construction.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that an LLM can rank uncertain business futures well without scenarios. This is the baseline any scenario scaffold has to beat, not assume.

source: Csaszar et al. (2026), aggregation and centaur results
finding: Simple averaging and voting did not beat the best single model, and adding a human did not help.
numbers: Best human (Expert 3) plus Gemini 2.5 Pro gives 0.67, below Gemini alone at 0.74. Ensembles (top three, all 20 LLMs, proprietary only, open only, humans only, grand) all fall below the best single model. Gemini + GPT-5 Mini gives 0.77 (+0.03, not significant).
limits: Ex post aggregation of independent predictions; interactive human-AI work not tested.
agent_relevance: Supports G4: pooling many weaker model samples does not give independence. Selecting the strongest single source dominates naive voting.

source: Csaszar et al. (2026), preregistered replication
finding: A second independent sample of projects gave a qualitatively similar pattern with lower absolute correlations. This is the only replication found in this subfield's LLM material.
numbers: 26 projects after 3 removed; 30.8% raised under $100 (vs 20.0% initially); 15.1% of pairs within $100 (vs 5.3%). Model ranking across the two samples: Spearman 0.54 over 19 models.
limits: LLM-only replication; humans were not rerun; ranking stability is only moderate (0.54).
agent_relevance: A model ordering found on one sample only half-transfers. Any scaffold gain on one set of items must be re-measured on a fresh set.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Time-R1: towards comprehensive temporal reasoning in LLMs. arXiv 2505.13508, stage 3 creative future scenario generation
finding: A 3B model was trained by RL on temporal tasks, then used with no extra training to write future news items. Plausibility was scored as best embedding similarity to real later news. All models scored in a narrow band, so the gain is small.
numbers: 8 themes, 3 items per prompt, greedy diversity filter to 5 per theme per month = 40 scenarios per month, Aug 2024 to Feb 2025, encoder all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Average AvgMaxSim: Time-R1 3B 48.90%; DeepSeek-V3 671B 48.81%; Time-R1 stage 2 only 47.93%; Qwen2.5-3B base 47.66%; DeepSeek-R1 671B 47.46%; DeepSeek-Distill-32B 47.12%.
limits: Spread is under 2 points with no significance test reported; cosine similarity to news is a weak plausibility proxy and rewards generic headlines.
agent_relevance: Shows scenario generation can be measured against later reality, and that scale and training barely move this metric. Do not read model size as scenario quality.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Time-R1, stages 1 and 2
finding: Stage 1 RL raised the overall temporal score of the base Qwen2.5-3B by about 171.6%. On future event prediction the 3B model beat much larger models.
numbers: Stage 2 average score: Time-R1 0.7780 vs DeepSeek-R1-671B 0.7503; Time-R1 stage-2-direct 0.7331. Fixed-reward variant plateaus near 0.70, curriculum reaches over 0.75.
limits: Task scores are the authors' own reward function. Training, not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: Context: training can beat size on temporal prediction. Our no-training approach cannot use this, so scaffold gains must be judged against plain prompts at equal compute.

source: Bertolotti & Mari (2025) An LLM-based Delphi study to predict GenAI evolution. arXiv 2502.21092
finding: LLM agents with randomly sampled expert personas ran a five-round Delphi on the future of generative AI, with an organiser agent writing follow-up questions. It surfaced geopolitics, economic gaps, regulation and ethics. Results changed run to run, and the same topics always came first.
numbers: Model gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, temperature 0.7, five rounds, 1 to 5 ratings, each configuration repeated 3 times; question dedupe by embedding similarity threshold; knowledge cutoff Oct 2023 versus study in Feb 2025.
limits: Persona voters drawn from one model are not independent; no human panel for comparison; authors flag cutoff, bias and sensitivity to initial conditions. This is Delphi, not Shell-style scenarios.
agent_relevance: Warning for G4: persona panels give breadth of wording, not independent views. Repeated runs vary, so any scenario set should be generated in more than one run and compared by code.

source: Bertolotti & Mari (2025), limits and fatigue claim
finding: Authors claim LLM panels remove respondent fatigue and allow many more questions, and that the order in which themes appear (geopolitics, inequality first) may reflect model preference, not the question set. They could not tell which.
numbers: Typical human Delphi: 15 to 20 participants. Panel size not tied to a human baseline.
limits: Untested claim that panel size improves reliability; no ground-truth forecast accuracy.
agent_relevance: Theme-order bias is a concrete failure to test for: the first scenario produced may reflect the model's habit, so shuffle or force the slot order.

source: Schoemaker, P.J.H. (1993) Multiple scenario development: its conceptual and behavioral foundation. Strategic Management Journal 14(3):193-213 (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Participant/observer account. Scenario planning differs from other tools by three traits: the script or narrative form, uncertainty across models rather than within one, and splitting a complex future into discrete states. It also discusses the need for diversity of views and simplicity.
numbers: Not extractable from the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; full paper behind a paywall in this run. Experimental claims (overconfidence reduced) not verified.
agent_relevance: Source of the three-trait definition; ties to our idea of discrete states with named rungs.

source: Phadnis, Caplice, Sheffi & Singh (2015) Effect of scenario planning on field experts' judgment of long-range investment decisions. Strategic Management Journal 36(9) (abstract via Crossref, DOI 10.1002/smj.2293)
finding: Three field experiments with field experts. Contrary to past findings, using multiple scenarios did not raise or lower confidence overall. Judgment moved with how the investment fared in the scenario used, shifted by prior confidence, and experts preferred more flexible options after using several scenarios.
numbers: Three field experiments; sample sizes and effect sizes not available from the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. It contradicts the older claim that scenarios reduce overconfidence.
agent_relevance: Most relevant human result: scenarios push judgment toward the scenario shown (an anchor) and toward flexibility. For us: show only the scenario skeleton needed and measure drift in the answer.

source: Hodgkinson & Wright (2002) Confronting strategic inertia in a top management team: learning from failure. Organization Studies 23(6) (abstract via Crossref)
finding: A reflective account of an attempt to use scenario planning and cognitive mapping with a top management team that was largely unsuccessful. The authors say the popular literature gives the impression that these techniques always work, and published failures are rare.
numbers: One top management team; qualitative.
limits: Abstract only; single case; authors were also the facilitators.
agent_relevance: A named failed application, a boundary condition: the method can fail where the group will not shift its view.

source: Healey & Hodgkinson (2009) Troubling futures: scenarios and scenario planning for organizational decision making. Oxford Handbook of Organizational Decision Making (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Argues from psychology that used unskillfully, scenarios can anchor and confine thinking, constructing them can induce or amplify bias, and they can change confidence and uncertainty disproportionately (misplaced optimism or threat rigidity). The negative emotion from scenarios may override their cognitive benefits.
numbers: None in abstract.
limits: Abstract only; a theory-based critique, not new data.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and G4: a scenario step can add bias. Use it only on a signal, and check the answer with something the scenarios were not fitted to (G3).

source: Goodwin & Wright (2001) Enhancing strategy evaluation in scenario planning: a role for decision analysis. Journal of Management Studies 38(1) (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Scenario planning avoids subjective probabilities, but strategy evaluation across scenarios is underdeveloped; informal evaluation can pick inferior strategies. They show how decision analysis (strategies scored across scenarios) can structure this step.
numbers: Not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: The missing step in the Shell funnel is scoring options against each scenario. Our program can compute a strategy-by-scenario table and pick by code (G5).

source: Ferrer i Pico et al. (2025) The Time Machine: future scenario generation through generative AI tools. Future Internet 17(1):48 (abstract via Crossref)
finding: A GPT-4 system produced future scenarios from input information, through three prompt versions and six trials. The authors report it fostered discussion on over 70% of generated scenarios and more than half contained new ideas, and say critical use is needed.
numbers: Six trials, 222 participants, three prompt versions; '+70%' discussion rate; '>50%' new ideas.
limits: Abstract only (publisher page blocked); outcome is self-rated usefulness in teams, no human-scenario baseline seen.
agent_relevance: Usefulness here is 'stimulated debate', not accuracy. A different target from ours.

source: Generative AI for Future Architecture Scenario Planning (2025, Research Square preprint 10.21203/rs.3.rs-6449315/v1; abstract via Crossref)
finding: GPT-4, Claude 2 and a LLaMA model each wrote a future-state enterprise architecture for three strategic scenarios and were compared with a human expert's design.
numbers: Coverage of scenario objectives 80 to 100% (GPT-4 near 100%, LLaMA about 80%); 10 to 15% more components than the expert (over-engineering); expert review score 7 to 8 out of 10; design time from weeks to seconds.
limits: Preprint, hypothetical mid-size enterprise, three scenarios, abstract only.
agent_relevance: The over-engineering tilt is a likely failure in LLM drafts: more parts, not better ones.

source: Cordova-Pozo & Rouwette (2023) Types of scenario planning and their effectiveness: a review of reviews. Futures 149:103153 (title and citation only; not opened)
finding: Review of reviews on scenario planning types and effectiveness. Polyscene cites it for the statement that evidence that scenario planning counters bias is mixed.
numbers: Not retrieved.
limits: Publisher blocked; no abstract came back. Content here is second-hand through Polyscene.
agent_relevance: The best available summary of effectiveness evidence; should be read in full before we claim any benefit from a reframe operator.

source: Kuhn & Sniezek (1996) Confidence and uncertainty in judgmental forecasting: differential effects of scenario presentation. J Behavioral Decision Making 9(4):231-247 (title only; not opened)
finding: The experimental paper that Phadnis et al. 2015 contrast with on confidence ('contrary to past findings' in their abstract; the link to this paper is my inference). Title says scenario presentation has differential effects on confidence and uncertainty in forecasts.
numbers: Not retrieved.
limits: No abstract returned by Crossref; no data checked.
agent_relevance: Pointer for the confidence-versus-scenario question (angle B should open it).

source: Meissner & Wulf (2013) Cognitive benefits of scenario planning: its impact on biases and decision quality. Technological Forecasting and Social Change 80 (title only; not opened)
finding: A study of scenario planning's effect on biases and decision quality. Content not retrieved here.
numbers: Not retrieved.
limits: No abstract returned; do not rely on it.
agent_relevance: Pointer for the bias-reduction evidence; angle B should open it.
